name: Romosozumab
lead: Romosozumab, sold as Evenity, is a humanized monoclonal antibody that binds and inhibits sclerostin, a protein made by bone-embedded osteocytes that restrains bone formation [1][2][26]. It is a prescription medicine given by subcutaneous injection to treat osteoporosis in postmenopausal women at high risk of fracture, and the US label limits use to 12 monthly doses, after which an antiresorptive drug is advised if therapy remains warranted [26]. It was approved in Japan in January 2019, the United States in April 2019 and the European Union in December 2019, and the FDA regards it as a first-in-class medication [1].

Because it both increases bone formation and, to a lesser extent, reduces bone resorption, it is often described as a dual-action agent [26][2]. Phase 3 trials found large reductions in vertebral fractures, but also more serious cardiovascular events than alendronate in one trial, and the label carries a boxed warning for myocardial infarction, stroke and cardiovascular death [1][26][6].

Romosozumab occasionally comes up in appearance-related discussion as a bone-building drug. Its approved use is osteoporosis only, and no published study has examined it for changing facial or skeletal structure in healthy people.

paras: The US label indicates romosozumab for postmenopausal women with osteoporosis at high fracture risk, defined by prior osteoporotic fracture, multiple risk factors, or failure of or intolerance to other therapy [26]. Japan also approved it for men, whereas it is not indicated for men or premenopausal women in the United States [2]. The Endocrine Society guideline update recommends anabolic therapy for postmenopausal women at very high fracture risk [16]. Reviews of osteoporosis therapy place romosozumab with teriparatide and abaloparatide as osteoanabolic agents for people needing rapid fracture-risk reduction [3][5][13].

There is no approved cosmetic use. The drug is sometimes mentioned in looksmaxxing contexts because it builds bone, but all published human research addresses osteoporosis and bone density in patients, and no study has tested effects on facial bone in healthy adults.

In the FRAME trial of 7,180 postmenopausal women with a hip or femoral-neck T score between -2.5 and -3.5, a year of monthly romosozumab followed by denosumab was compared with placebo then denosumab [7]; a 73 percent lower risk of new vertebral fracture at 12 months was reported, with the benefit maintained after the switch to denosumab [1][2]. In the ARCH trial of 4,093 women with osteoporosis and a fragility fracture, 12 months of romosozumab followed by alendronate was compared with alendronate alone, with about a 48 to 50 percent lower vertebral fracture risk over 24 months [6][1][2]. A sub-analysis of ARCH reported better lumbar spine bone strength parameters than with alendronate [11].

A 2022 meta-analysis of trials in postmenopausal osteoporosis found significant reductions in vertebral, nonvertebral and clinical fractures and increases in bone mineral density at the lumbar spine, total hip and femoral neck [4]. A phase 3 trial in women transitioning from oral bisphosphonates compared romosozumab with teriparatide for bone density [14]. A phase 3 trial in men with osteoporosis evaluated bone mineral density outcomes [8], and a phase 2 trial in women with low bone mass established the dose-response relationship [10]. A 2026 non-inferiority trial (LIDA) compared 3 months with 12 months of treatment [9].

Evidence comes from patients with osteoporosis rather than people seeking a cosmetic effect. Key randomised trials are the FRAME placebo-controlled trial [7], the ARCH comparison with alendronate [6][11], the comparison with teriparatide after bisphosphonate therapy [14], a phase 3 trial in men [8], a phase 2 dose-finding study [10], and the LIDA duration trial [9]. A network meta-analysis compared pharmacological therapies for fracture prevention in postmenopausal women [17]. The commentary 'Unmasking romosozumab' discussed the drug's cardiovascular signal [12].

Registered studies include trials in postmenopausal women in India, transition from alendronate, patients with breast cancer, multiple myeloma and renal impairment or dialysis, combination with denosumab, comparison with denosumab in long-term glucocorticoid users, and a phase 3 trial in children and adolescents with osteogenesis imperfecta [18][19][20][21][23][22][24][25].

Common effects are joint pain, headache and injection-site reactions [1][2]. The US boxed warning states that romosozumab may increase the risk of myocardial infarction, stroke and cardiovascular death, and that it should not be started in anyone who has had a heart attack or stroke within the previous year [26]. In the ARCH trial more patients on romosozumab than alendronate had serious cardiovascular events (0.8 versus 0.3 percent), a difference not seen in the placebo-controlled FRAME trial, and a large real-world study found fewer cardiovascular events than with other osteoanabolic therapies [1][6][7]. Observational data reported as of 2025 suggest no increased cardiovascular risk compared with other osteoporosis treatments, while monitoring continues [2].

Other label warnings cover hypersensitivity reactions, hypocalcaemia (calcium and vitamin D supplementation is advised), osteonecrosis of the jaw and atypical femoral fractures [26]. Real-world data indicate jaw osteonecrosis was very rare during one year of use [1]. Romosozumab is not indicated for women of reproductive potential; in rats, high exposures produced skeletal abnormalities in offspring [26].

Sclerostin, encoded by the SOST gene and produced mainly by osteocytes, binds LRP5 and LRP6 and blocks Wnt signalling, suppressing osteoblast activity [2]. By neutralising sclerostin, romosozumab restores Wnt/beta-catenin signalling, which increases bone formation and, via effects such as reduced RANKL expression, also lowers resorption [2][26]. Animal studies showed new bone formation on trabecular and cortical surfaces [26]. Bone-density gains are greatest in the spine and also seen at the hip [2].

As an IgG2 antibody, romosozumab is cleared by target-mediated binding and by catabolism into peptides and amino acids rather than by cytochrome P450 metabolism, and peaks in the blood several days after injection with an effective half-life of roughly 12.8 days after repeated monthly doses, according to one summary [2].

Romosozumab was discovered by Chiroscience, which was acquired by Celltech (owned since 2004 by UCB), and Celltech partnered with Amgen on development in 2002 [1]. Approval came in Japan in January 2019, the United States on 9 April 2019 and the EU in December 2019 [1][2]. The UK's National Institute for Health and Care Excellence decided to recommend it for use in England and Wales [1]. It was listed among the novel antibodies receiving first approval in the 2019 cohort in the annual 'Antibodies to watch' review [15].

Evenity is a prescription product administered under clinical supervision. No looksmaxxing forum material specific to romosozumab is documented in the research record; discussion of bone-building drugs for appearance more broadly is described under teriparatide.
